title: Environmental Control Extends Beyond Quantum Dephasing in Exciton Energy Transfer
authors: Junhua Zhou, Tianrui Chen, Dehao Yuan, Enhu He, Vandana Tiwari, Maxim Gelin, Francoise Remacle, R. J. Dwayne Miller, Fulu Zheng, Ajay Jha, Hong-Guang Duan
abstract: Excitation-energy transfer underpins the conversion of light into usable energy in photosynthetic organisms and serves as a paradigm for evolutionary optimized transport in open quantum systems. Although this process is often described as incoherent thermally assisted hopping, such descriptions become inadequate when electronic coupling, vibronic interactions and environmental fluctuations occur on comparable energy scales. Determining how the environment controls transport therefore remains a fundamental challenge. Here, we use temperature-dependent 2DES to investigate energy transfer in the photosynthetic antenna protein allophycocyanin over the range 10 - 296 K. The dominant $β\rightarrow α$ transfer step exhibits a pronounced non-monotonic temperature dependence: the transfer time decreases from 400 fs at 10 K to 200 fs near 30- 40 K before increasing again to 400 fs at 296 K. In contrast, the homogeneous optical dephasing time decreases monotonically across the same temperature range. To interpret these observations, we model APC as a vibronically coupled excitonic dimer interacting with a structured environment and solve the dynamics using hierarchical equations of motion. Conventional fixed-bath models, including Drude-Lorentz and explicit intermolecular-mode spectral densities, fail to reproduce the observed turnover. Quantitative agreement is obtained only when the low-frequency sector of the environmental spectral density is allowed to anharmonically evolve strongly with temperature, while the high-frequency bath remains essentially unchanged. More broadly, these findings demonstrate that transport efficiency is controlled not simply by the magnitude of environmental fluctuations, but by the distribution of environmental spectral weight across frequency space, providing new experimental constraints on theories of molecular transport in complex quantum environments.
summary: This work investigates energy transfer in the APC protein, finding that the transfer rate shows a complex, non-monotonic temperature dependence. This behavior cannot be explained by simple dephasing models, necessitating a detailed treatment of the environment's low-frequency spectral weight. The findings demonstrate that the specific frequency distribution of environmental coupling, not just the overall fluctuation strength, controls quantum energy transport efficiency.
main_problem: The study addresses how environmental fluctuations control excitation energy transfer in photosynthetic complexes, moving beyond simple models like incoherent hopping.
main_result: The energy transfer time exhibits a non-monotonic temperature dependence (minimum near 30-40 K), which contrasts sharply with the monotonic decrease of the homogeneous optical dephasing time.
method: The research combines temperature-dependent 2DES measurements with advanced open-quantum system simulations using the Hierarchical Equations of Motion (HEOM).
model_or_system: The system is the Allophycocyanin (APC) protein, modeled as a vibronically coupled excitonic dimer interacting with a structured, temperature-dependent environment.
key_observables: Energy transfer time ($ eta ightarrow \alpha$), homogeneous optical dephasing time, and the environmental spectral density distribution.
important_parameters: Temperature range (10 K to 296 K), electronic coupling strength ($J$), and the frequency distribution of environmental spectral weight.
main_assumptions: Conventional fixed-bath models fail; quantitative agreement requires allowing the low-frequency sector of the environmental spectral density to evolve anharmonically with temperature.
figures_summary: Figures compare the non-monotonic energy transfer turnover against the monotonic dephasing decrease, illustrating that low-frequency environmental modes govern the transport efficiency.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical problem using 2DES experiments across a wide temperature range, develops a detailed vibronic model, and uses HEOM simulations to reproduce the key non-monotonic temperature dependence, contrasting it with simpler dephasing metrics.
why_interesting: It provides a detailed, quantitative example of how environmental spectral weight distribution, rather than just the magnitude of fluctuations, dictates quantum transport rates in complex biological systems, which is highly relevant to open quantum system dynamics.
